overview: Michael Hill is a specialty jewellery retailer founded in Whangarei, New Zealand in 1979 by Sir Michael Hill, now operating 282-287 stores across Australia, New Zealand and Canada under the Michael Hill and Bevilles banners (legacy brands TenSevenSeven, Medley and Watches Galore are being wound down/absorbed by end of FY26). The Group is dual-listed on the NZX (MHJ.NZ, quoted in NZD) and ASX (primary listing, MHJ.AX), but reports its financial statements in AUD on a 52/53-week fiscal year ending late June. It is a micro-cap (~NZ$160-180m market value) with a founding-family shareholding still above 45% of the register.

business_model.summary: Michael Hill designs, manufactures (via its own Brisbane-based manufacturing/wholesale operation) and retails jewellery, watches and related services through company-operated stores and digital channels. Revenue is overwhelmingly transactional (single jewellery purchases, largely bridal, gifting and self-purchase), supplemented by a meaningful recurring/deferred-revenue stream from Professional Care Plans (PCP) — extended-care/warranty contracts sold alongside jewellery. PCP revenue is deferred and recognised over the life of the plan (historically offered in 3- or 10-year terms), so it smooths earnings and represents a high-margin annuity-like profit pool layered on top of the core hardware sale; the Board and investor materials flag it as the group's 'highest-engagement service' with 'stronger repeat purchasing behaviour' and 'longer lifetime brand relationships.' The FY25 annual report and prior filings do not break out PCP revenue/deferred balance as a separate disclosed line in the extracted text reviewed — the deferred revenue balance sheet quantum could not be independently verified from the excerpts read and should be checked in the full financial statement notes before being used as a standalone valuation input.
business_model.customer_type: B2C mass/mid-market specialty jewellery consumer; bridal, gifting and self-purchase segments; loyalty base of 3.2m+ members generating over 4 in 5 transactions
business_model.geographic_mix: FY2025 revenue (local currency): Australia A$364.1m (incl. Bevilles), Canada C$162.4m, New Zealand NZ$109.0m; group reported revenue A$643.7m. Store count at FY25 year-end: 287 (AU 160 incl. 37 Bevilles, Canada 82, NZ 45); by April 2026 investor day, 282 stores (AU 158 incl. 36 Bevilles, Canada 81, NZ 43).

competitive_position.market_position: Mid-market/'accessible modern luxury' positioning in a fragmented industry; per IBISWorld, Prouds The Jewellers holds more Australian watch-and-jewellery-retailing market share than Michael Hill, with Richemont Australia also a larger competitor by some measures. Michael Hill's newly acquired Bevilles brand competes at the value end against Prouds and department-store/mass jewellery counters. In Canada, management explicitly frames Michael Hill as the 'growth engine' with 'lower share than AU/NZ' and 'significant runway,' while New Zealand is described as the company's most mature, highest-brand-awareness market where it holds the #1 position.

moat_factors.description: In-house design and Brisbane manufacturing/wholesale operations let the company control product economics and react to metal price volatility rather than relying solely on third-party vendors; management explicitly cites this as a lever for 'sustained pricing power and resilient margins.'

282+ stores across three countries function as fulfilment nodes (majority of digital sales are collected in-store via click & collect), a structural advantage versus pure online / lab-grown-diamond disruptors that lack a trial/fitting experience for bridal purchases.

3.2m+ loyalty members generate over 80% of transactions; 'Brilliance' top-tier members show materially higher average transaction value, gross profit dollars and gross margin than non-members. PCP, repairs, cleaning and engraving create repeat store visits and incremental revenue beyond the initial jewellery sale.
46-year-old brand founded by the recently-deceased Sir Michael Hill; high brand awareness in New Zealand and Australia, less so in Canada where brand-building is a stated multi-year priority.
Mid-sized (~$650m revenue) relative to global players like Pandora and Signet; scale is a disadvantage versus Pandora's global sourcing but an advantage versus small independents.

weaknesses: Structurally thinner competitive moat than franchise/network-effect businesses — jewellery is a commoditised, price-comparable, big-ticket discretionary purchase

Bevilles acquisition (A$46.1m, completed June 2023) has underperformed the original investment thesis: 'strategic drift' post-acquisition (head-office relocation, technology re-platforming, commercial-model changes, 'underperforming expansion') led to a $7.4m non-cash brand-intangible impairment in FY25 against an original ~$20m intangible carrying value, and store network expansion has been paused pending a 'Reset'
New Zealand segment same-store sales fell -5.5% in FY25 (only turning positive, +1.8%, in H1 FY26) — a mature, low-growth market requiring 'network optimisation' (rightsizing the tail of the fleet)

No hedging disclosure of gold price exposure identified in the filings reviewed — margin protection appears to rely on pricing/product-mix agility rather than financial hedges, which is a less certain buffer in a fast-rising commodity environment

Two consecutive years of leadership disruption: sudden death of CEO Daniel Bracken (Feb 2025) and passing of founder/director Sir Michael Hill (29 July 2025), both requiring board and executive transition in a short window

growth_drivers: New CEO Jonathan Waecker (ex-Disney, Yahoo, The Warehouse Group; started 27 Aug 2025) has driven an 'operational reset' - simplified pricing/promotional architecture, tighter product focus, data-driven decision-making - with early results (H1 FY26 and Q3 FY26 trading updates) showing sales growth returning across all three segments with margins sustained

Canada is explicitly positioned as the primary growth engine: record same-store sales in FY25 (+4.4%) and accelerating further in FY26 (H1 +6.1%, Q3 +11.3%); store ambition raised to ~85-90 stores from 81 currently, with 'significant runway' cited given lower brand penetration than AU/NZ

Brand portfolio simplification from 5 brands to 2 (Michael Hill + Bevilles) by end of FY26 - winding down TenSevenSeven, Medley and Watches Galore - intended to reduce complexity and redirect capital/management attention to the two brands with the clearest value proposition

Bevilles 'Reset, Perform, Grow' stage-gated turnaround: early FY26 trading metrics (same-store sales, GP%, GP$) turned positive in Q3 FY26 after a soft H1; further store rollout is explicitly gated behind proof of a repeatable, profitable unit economics model before re-expansion

Digital/omni-channel growth outpacing total sales growth, with digital margins in line with store margins and most digital sales fulfilled via click & collect (supporting rather than cannibalising the store network); management sizes the digital opportunity at '2x-3x' current levels, concentrated in Canada then Australia

TenSevenSeven's bespoke/custom bridal proposition (average transaction value >4x standard Michael Hill bridal ATV) is being scaled as an in-store trial across the core Michael Hill network - a potential average-transaction-value and margin lever

New in-country distribution centres (Auckland DC commissioned early FY26, completing a three-country in-house fulfilment network) targeted at reducing logistics cost and improving digital delivery speed

Management's stated medium-term ambition is a 10% group EBIT margin (from ~2.4% comparable EBIT margin in FY25) via four levers: store productivity, diversified revenue growth, gross margin improvement, and operating leverage - a substantial re-rating opportunity if delivered, though currently unquantified/undated by fiscal year
Product innovation in Men's, Basics, Bridal and premium lab-grown diamonds (alongside natural diamonds) targeted as 'opportunity growth categories'

business.risk: Gold and silver input cost inflation
business.description: Gold has traded at multiple record highs through FY25 and into FY26. Management states gross margin has been held 'broadly flat' (~60.5% FY25, ~61.2% H1 FY26) only by offsetting cost increases with 'agile pricing discipline,' product/mix management and supplier partnerships - there is no evidence in the filings reviewed of a formal financial hedging program for gold, so margin protection is entirely a pricing/execution outcome that could fail if gold volatility outpaces the company's ability to reprice or if promotional intensity increases in a soft consumer environment.

A$46.1m acquisition (2023) has already taken a $7.4m non-cash brand impairment in FY25; the 'Reset' is a stage-gated multi-year turnaround (Gate 1: return to performance; Gate 2: prove sustained SSS/GP growth; Gate 3: expansion decision) - failure to clear these gates could mean further capital is trapped in an underperforming asset, and additional impairment is possible if the reset stalls.

business.risk: Structural competitive/margin pressure from lab-grown diamonds
business.description: Lab-grown diamond wholesale prices have fallen ~85-90% since 2018-2020 as global production capacity surged; this compresses the price gap versus natural stones, pressures average selling prices/margins across the industry (De Beers parent Anglo American took a $2.3bn impairment on the natural-diamond business in 2025), and could reduce mined-diamond bridal average transaction values over time. MHJ's FY25 annual report explicitly flags 'increasing price gaps between mined and laboratory created diamonds' as a top risk, noting both product types feature in its range as a mitigant.

Two leadership shocks in five months (CEO Daniel Bracken's sudden death, Feb 2025; founder Sir Michael Hill's passing, Jul 2025) required an interim CEO period and a global search culminating in external hire Jonathan Waecker (started Aug 2025) - execution risk remains elevated during a multi-year strategic reset under new leadership with limited jewellery-sector-specific tenure.

NZ same-store sales fell -5.5% in FY25 before recovering to +1.8% in H1 FY26 and +7.1% in the FY26 Q3 update; management's stated strategy is 'defend & optimise' rather than growth, including rightsizing the store tail - a mature market ceiling limits this segment's contribution to group growth.
FY25 annual report flags rising theft and violence risk in stores during periods of financial hardship, requiring dedicated security investment and an executive taskforce.

financial.risk: No dividend and history of suspension
financial.description: No interim or final dividend was paid for FY2024 or FY2025 (the FY2024 interim of 1.75cps was the last dividend paid, and even that followed a FY2023 final of 3.5cps that was itself cut from prior levels); Board cited 'continued compressed earnings in FY25' and a 'commitment to prudent investment in operating and capital expenditure in FY26' as the reason for withholding the FY25 final dividend. This is a major break from the company's history as a consistent dividend payer and removes an income-investor support level from the stock.

financial.risk: Net debt / seasonal working capital reliance
financial.description: FY25 closed with net debt of A$41.9m (FY24: A$38.7m); the company temporarily increased its debt facility by $20m for four months to fund Christmas seasonal working capital. H1 FY26 showed a swing to net CASH of $20.7m (a $30.5m improvement versus the prior-year net debt position), aided by inventory reduction (-$11.3m) and new supplier terms - a positive but recent and reversible trend given the historically negative net cash position and seasonal swings.

Inventory closed FY25 at $199.1m (FY24: $195.8m) even as unit volumes were actively managed down, reflecting record gold prices baked into carrying cost; a sharp gold price reversal could create inventory/margin risk, though H1 FY26 showed inventory reduced by $11.3m (-5.3%) via working-capital discipline.

financial.risk: Debt refinancing completed on improved terms
financial.description: H1 FY26 disclosed the existing facility was refinanced for an additional two years with long-term partner ANZ, adding a new lender (CBA) - a de-risking event, not a live concern, but notable given the prior reliance on a single-bank facility.

regulatory.risk: Consumer protection / extended warranty (PCP) compliance history
regulatory.description: Michael Hill was fined NZ$169,000 by the NZ Commerce Commission in 2018 for Professional Care Plan (extended warranty) disclosure failures and for misleadingly adding PCP cost to a bracelet price without customer knowledge. While historical, this establishes PCP - a material and growing services revenue line - as an area of active regulatory scrutiny in the jurisdictions the company operates in.

The Group was exempt from NZ climate-disclosure rules in FY25 given its ASX primary listing, but acknowledges upcoming mandatory Australian Sustainability Reporting Standards disclosure from FY26, adding compliance cost.
Standard multinational retailer risk disclosed in the FY25 annual report relating to transfer pricing policy across AU/NZ/Canada operations.

macro.description: Jewellery is a highly discretionary, big-ticket purchase category; FY25 explicitly cites 'persistent cost of living pressures and significant global uncertainty' weighing on consumer confidence in AU/NZ/Canada, and FY26 Q3 commentary flags 'continued monitoring of rapidly evolving consumer headwinds and increased volatility going into Q4 and FY27' - despite recent same-store-sales recovery, the macro backdrop remains a live risk to sustaining momentum.

macro.risk: Gold and precious metal price volatility
macro.description: Record gold prices through FY25-FY26 are the single largest identified cost pressure; further increases would test the company's ability to reprice without demand destruction, particularly given an already 'heightened promotional environment.'

Reports in AUD but generates meaningful revenue in NZD and CAD; currency translation affects reported group results even when local-currency segment performance is stable or improving (management consistently reports segment results 'in local currency' to strip this out).

Both a direct effect (net debt/facility interest cost, though the group moved to a net cash position at H1 FY26) and an indirect effect via mortgage-rate-driven household discretionary spending capacity in Australia, NZ and Canada.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Australian jewellery market is low-growth/mature (~0.5-3% CAGR depending on source) and fragmented; industry-wide pressure from lab-grown diamond price deflation is reshaping category economics even as unit demand for lab-grown stones grows sharply (lab-grown share of diamond center-stone sales rose from ~12% in 2019 to ~52% in 2024 per industry data)
macro_factors.cyclicality: High - jewellery (particularly non-bridal, gifting and self-purchase categories) is one of the more cyclical/discretionary retail categories, sensitive to consumer confidence, employment and interest-rate-driven household budgets; bridal demand is comparatively more resilient (a 'life milestone' purchase) which management explicitly leans into as a stabilising segment
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate - direct impact via net debt funding cost (currently modest given the shift to a net cash position at H1 FY26) and material indirect impact via consumer discretionary spending capacity across all three operating geographies

recent_developments.event: CEO Daniel Bracken passed away suddenly; CFO Andrew Lowe appointed Interim CEO (6 March 2025) while a global search for a permanent CEO was conducted.

Full year results: revenue A$643.7m (down 0.2%), reported EBIT A$18.9m (up 32.5%, boosted by a $3.0m favourable litigation outcome), comparable EBIT A$15.3m (down from $15.9m), statutory NPAT A$2.1m (FY24: A$0.5m loss). Result includes a $7.4m non-cash Bevilles brand intangible impairment. Gross margin held at 60.5% (FY24: 60.6%) despite record gold prices. No final dividend declared.
Founder and non-executive director Sir Michael Hill passed away, aged 86, shortly after taking a leave of absence from the Board (14 April 2025).

Jonathan Waecker (previously Chief Customer & Sales Officer, The Warehouse Group; prior roles at Disney and Yahoo) appointed CEO, commencing 27 August 2025; Andrew Lowe reverted to CFO and supply-chain role.
FY2025 annual results released; Chair Rob Fyfe confirmed no interim or final dividend declared for FY2025, citing compressed earnings and a commitment to prudent FY26 capex/opex investment.

H1 FY2026 results (26 weeks to 28 Dec 2025): comparable EBIT $31.0m (up 28.6%), revenue $371.0m (up 3.0%), group same-store sales +3.8% (Canada +6.1%, Australia +4.8%, NZ +1.8% - first positive NZ SSS after prior-year declines). Gross margin broadly flat at 61.2% despite record gold/silver costs. Swing to net cash position of $20.7m (from $9.8m net debt a year earlier). No interim dividend declared, but Board explicitly signalled intent to resume dividends at the FY26 full-year result, subject to trading conditions continuing. Debt facility refinanced for two more years with ANZ, adding CBA as a new lender.

Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC, NZ's state accident insurer/investor) disclosed a substantial shareholder notice with a 2.48% stake in Michael Hill, subsequently built up materially through 2026.

ACC increased its stake to 5.819% via ASX market purchases; Michael Hill hosted an Investor Day (14 April 2026) in Brisbane detailing the CEO's operational reset framework, brand simplification from 5 to 2 brands (Michael Hill + Bevilles; winding down TenSevenSeven, Medley and Watches Galore by end of FY26), a medium-term ambition of a 10% group EBIT margin, and confirmed intent to return to dividends at the FY26 full-year result.

recent_developments.date: 2026-04 (FY26 Q3 update, within Investor Day materials)
recent_developments.event: Group sales up 3.8% in Q3; group same-store sales up 4.6% (Australia +5.5%, Canada +11.3%, New Zealand +7.1%); gross margins broadly flat versus prior year; management flagged 'rapidly evolving consumer headwinds and increased volatility going into Q4 and FY27.'

FY2026 full-year trading update: group sales $654.7m (up 2.0% reported, +3.9% constant currency); same-store sales +3% (+5.2% constant currency); comparable EBIT guided to $22-24m, representing 44-57% growth versus FY25's $15.3m. Full FY2026 results scheduled for 28 August 2026, at which the Board's dividend decision will be confirmed.

guidance.as_of: FY2026 Trading Update, 31 July 2026 (full results due 28 August 2026)
guidance.fiscal_year: FY2026 (53 weeks to 28 June 2026, per typical MHJ retail calendar - exact week count not confirmed in extracted filings)

items.vs_prior: raised/reaffirmed strong growth vs FY25 actual
items.notes: Represents 44% to 57% growth versus FY25 comparable EBIT of $15.3m; guidance issued via ASX/NZX trading update ahead of the 28 August 2026 full-year result.
Up 2.0% reported / 3.9% constant currency versus FY25's $643.7m; same-store sales +3% reported / +5.2% constant currency for the full year.

items.vs_prior: raised from nil (FY24 and FY25 paid zero dividends)
items.notes: Board has repeated at both the H1 FY26 result and the April 2026 Investor Day that it 'intends to return to dividends at the FY26 full year results, subject to trading conditions continuing' and in line with the Company's stated dividend policy of 50%-75% of Adjusted NPAT payout ratio. This is not a locked commitment - it is explicitly conditional.

No specific percentage guided; management's repeated message through FY26 quarterly updates has been that gross margin is being held roughly flat (~60-61%) despite record gold/silver costs, via pricing discipline and product mix.

items.vs_prior: new - first articulated at April 2026 Investor Day
items.notes: Framed as an aspirational, multi-year target built on four levers (store productivity, diversified revenue growth, gross margin improvement, operating leverage), not a near-term FY guidance figure. FY25 comparable EBIT margin was ~2.4% of revenue, implying a very large gap to close.

items.vs_prior: new target disclosed at Investor Day
items.notes: Growth via disciplined store openings in high-traffic malls in underdeveloped provinces.
Strategy is disciplined lease renewals, exiting underperforming locations, not net expansion.
Focus on refurbishment and rightsizing the tail rather than growth.

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Jonathan Waecker: framework of 'Operational Clarity, Customer Focus and Data Discipline' is 'working' with 'sales growth returned, margins sustained' in the first six months of his tenure. Chair Rob Fyfe emphasised 'disciplined capital allocation' with intent to return to dividends at FY26 full year 'subject to trading conditions continuing.' Management consistently flags 'rapidly evolving consumer headwinds and increased volatility going into Q4 and FY27' as a caveat even while reporting improving same-store sales trends - guidance should be read as cautiously optimistic rather than a confident multi-year outlook.

bull_case: New CEO-led operational reset is showing concrete, accelerating evidence in the numbers: comparable EBIT guided up 44-57% for FY26 to $22-24m, with same-store sales growth turning positive and broadening across all three segments (including New Zealand, the previous laggard) through H1 and Q3 FY26

Balance sheet has swung from net debt to net cash ($20.7m at H1 FY26 vs $9.8m net debt a year prior), debt facility refinanced on improved terms with an added lender, and inventory has been reduced even as gold costs rose - de-risking the capital structure ahead of a likely dividend resumption at the 28 August 2026 FY26 result

Canada is a genuine, underpenetrated growth market (record same-store sales every recent period, accelerating to low-double-digit growth by Q3 FY26) with a credible medium-term store-count expansion plan

Gross margin has proven resilient (~60-61%) through a record gold price cycle via pricing/mix discipline, evidencing some pricing power and design/vertical-integration advantages that management is now trying to convert into an ambitious 10% EBIT margin target (from ~2.4% in FY25) - even partial delivery would be a substantial re-rating catalyst

Brand-portfolio simplification (5 brands to 2) and the stage-gated Bevilles reset reduce organisational complexity and management distraction, while a very depressed valuation (micro-cap, ~NZ$0.42-0.45, well below the ~2021-2022 premium-brand-repositioning-era highs) already appears to price in a good deal of past disappointment; rising institutional interest (ACC's stake build to 5.8%+ through 2026) is a positive signal
bear_case: Dividend suspension across FY2024 and FY2025 (the last payment was the FY2024 interim of 1.75cps) removes the income-support underpinning the stock previously enjoyed; the Board's 'intent' to resume at the FY26 full year is explicitly conditional on trading conditions continuing, and could disappoint if Q4 FY26/H1 FY27 momentum stalls

Record and potentially still-rising gold and silver prices are a persistent structural cost headwind for a jewellery retailer with no disclosed financial hedging program; margin protection currently depends entirely on repricing/product-mix execution in an already 'heightened promotional environment,' which is a fragile buffer if the consumer discretionary backdrop weakens further (management itself flags 'increased volatility going into Q4 and FY27')

Bevilles remains an unproven, stage-gated turnaround after a $7.4m non-cash impairment and a 'strategic drift' period post-acquisition; further capital or management time invested in Bevilles carries real execution risk before Gate 2/3 (sustained profitability, expansion case) are proven

Leadership discontinuity (two departures via death - CEO Bracken and founder Sir Michael Hill - within five months of each other) forced a rushed CEO transition; the current strategy, still less than a year old under an externally-hired CEO with no prior jewellery-sector experience, is unproven over a full cycle

Structural industry risk from lab-grown diamond price deflation (down ~85-90% since 2018-2020) could progressively compress average transaction values and bridal-category economics industry-wide, a risk the company explicitly discloses but cannot fully control or hedge; combined with a low-growth, fragmented, highly cyclical discretionary retail category and larger-scale competitors (Pandora, Prouds, Lovisa), the long-term moat is modest
data_gaps_and_caveats: PCP (Professional Care Plan) deferred revenue balance and annual revenue contribution were not disclosed as a standalone line in the FY2025 annual report sections and H1 FY2026 half-year report reviewed (financial statement notes on revenue disaggregation/deferred revenue were not fully read in this pass) - the description of its economics here draws on investor-day qualitative commentary and a historical NZ Commerce Commission enforcement case, not a verified current dollar figure.

No explicit gold/precious-metal hedging policy disclosure (e.g., forward contracts, hedge accounting for commodity price risk) was located in the filings reviewed; only FX cash-flow hedging (USD purchases) was historically referenced in web search results from an older annual report. This should be confirmed directly against the FY2025 annual report's financial risk management note before concluding the company is fully unhedged on gold.

Total current shares on issue (~384.8m per third-party data) and the precise current combined Hill family shareholding percentage (directors' register shows Sir Michael Hill's estate at 148,330,600 shares and Emma Hill at 167,487,526 shares as of the FY2025 annual report date, together already >45% of ~384.8m shares on issue) were cross-checked against web sources (citing ~46.9% combined) but not independently recomputed from a primary substantial-shareholder notice; treat as directionally correct but not to-the-decimal verified. Note Sir Michael Hill's shares are now held via his estate following his July 2025 passing, which may be a future overhang/estate-planning consideration not addressed in the filings reviewed.

Current share price (~NZ$0.42-0.45 per recent web data / ~A$0.34-0.39 on ASX) and resulting market capitalisation were sourced from web search snapshots rather than a live quote at time of writing; given the FY26 result is due 28 August 2026, price and market cap should be treated as approximate and time-sensitive.

No evidence of a live takeover approach, formal strategic review, or capital-return/buyback program was found in the sources reviewed; ACC's stake build to 5.8%+ appears to be a passive/institutional accumulation rather than disclosed activism, but this should be monitored via NZX/ASX substantial-holder notices.
